title: Networks: why, what size, and which model

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Why devices are networked; LANs and WANs; the client-server and peer-to-peer models; and thin and thick clients.

blocks.heading: Why computers are networked
blocks.text: Computers work alone until they are connected. A network is two or more computing devices joined so that they can communicate and share data and resources, and the connection changes what each machine can do. Files move between users directly instead of travelling on a storage device by hand. Hardware is shared: one printer serves a whole office, one file store holds the organisation's records, because each device on the network can reach them. Management becomes central: on a network with a server, backup runs once for everyone and security is administered in one place instead of machine by machine. Communication joins the list: two users work on one document across the network, a message reaches a colleague at the next desk, and a learner in the computer room submits work to a teacher's marking folder without leaving a chair. The devices that make a network - the switches, routers and access points met later in this topic - each do one job in moving data from a sender to a receiver, which is the infrastructure the sharing rests on. The benefits come with costs, and the costs are worth counting: a network needs hardware and cabling, someone to run it, and a fault in a shared device can stop many users at once, where a stand-alone machine fails alone.

blocks.heading: LAN and WAN
blocks.text: Networks come in two sizes. A local area network (LAN) covers one small site - one building, one campus - and is owned and managed by the organisation that uses it: the school's computer room, the office's floor. The devices on it are close together, and the links between them belong to the organisation. A wide area network (WAN) covers a large geographical area, joining sites across a country or the world, and it uses long-distance links leased from communication providers, because no organisation lays its own cable between towns. The internet is the largest example of a WAN: a network of networks spanning the globe, built from countless LANs joined by long-distance links. The two sizes meet in every organisation with branches: each branch runs its own LAN on its own site, and a WAN joins the LANs together. When a bank's Windhoek branch sends a record to Oshakati, the record travels inside a LAN, across a WAN, and inside another LAN, and each part of the journey uses the kind of network that fits that stretch. Ownership is the second mark of the difference: the bank's branch owns its own LAN's switches and cables, but nobody owns the whole internet - providers own stretches of it, and everyone's packets travel across one another's links, which is what paying a provider buys a place on.

blocks.heading: Client-server and peer-to-peer
blocks.text: Two models describe who does what on a networked system. In the client-server model, server computers provide services, files and resources, and client computers request and use them: the file server stores everyone's documents, the print server queues everyone's printing, and the client asks. Because the server holds the resources, it can control them: one account per user, one place for a backup, one point where security is set. In the peer-to-peer model there is no special server: each computer is equal, and any of them can share its own files, printer or connection with the others, acting as both client and server as needed. Each model earns its place. A client-server network suits organisations where central control matters - a school with learners' records, a firm with one file store - and it pays for it with the server's cost and the need to manage it. A peer-to-peer network suits a few machines in one room: nothing to buy beyond the machines and the cable, no manager needed, but each user is responsible for their own machine's shared data, and there is no central backup unless someone organises it. Justifying a model means matching it to the situation: count the machines, ask who is responsible for what, and ask whether the data is worth a server.

blocks.heading: Thin client and thick client
blocks.text: Clients themselves come in two forms. A thin client is a computer that depends on a server for processing and storage: it sends the user's requests over the network and displays the results, while the server does the work and holds the files. A thick client (also called a fat client) is a full computer: it runs its own applications locally, keeps its own files on its own storage, and needs no server to function. The differences reach into cost and security. Thin clients are cheap to buy and cheap to administer: software lives on the server and is updated once, data stays on the server, and a broken thin client is simply swapped. But a thin client without its server is a door with no house: it cannot work, and a network fault stops every thin client at once. Thick clients cost more and must each be maintained, updated and secured, and their data sits wherever their users have left it; in exchange they keep working without a server, they run demanding applications at their own pace, and a slow network does not throttle them.

blocks.heading: Worked example: choosing for a school office
blocks.text: A school office has five computers and one printer, and the office keeps the school's records. Which model, and which kind of client? Model first: records matter and must be backed up, and five users need controlled access to them, so the client-server model fits - one server holds the records, each staff account reaches them, backup runs on the server, and the printer hangs off the network for all five machines. Peer-to-peer would scatter the records over five machines with five owners and no central backup, which the records' importance rules out. Client kind second: the office's work is records and letters, not design or video, so the demands are light; thin clients keep all data on the server, which suits records that must not be lost, and one old machine that cannot run new software can still serve as a thin client because the server does the work. Had the office edited video, thick clients would have won the second choice, because rendering video over a network is slower than running it locally. Had the office been three friends sharing a flat's one printer, the whole reasoning would have flipped: three machines and nothing worth a server make peer-to-peer the sensible answer, which shows the justification runs from the situation, not from a favourite model.
